newsitem.title: INDIA: Freedom is fleeting for master criminal Sobhraj.
newsitem.headline: Freedom is fleeting for master criminal Sobhraj.

text.p: Convict Charles Sobhraj won release from prison on Monday after more than two decades behind bars but Indian police quickly detained the notorious criminal, cutting short his freedom.

Chief metropolitan magistrate Prem Kumar ordered Sobhraj released on bail from Tihar jail after Sobhraj, whose exploits across Asia have been the basis of two books, provided a personal bond worth 30,000 rupees ($835).
Minutes later, dozens of police surrounded Sobhraj as he left the Tis Hizari courts and detained him because he did not have up-to-date identity papers.
"They have again arrested him because he did not have any valid documents," said Amit Sharma, one of his lawyers.
Surrounded by police but without handcuffs, Sobhraj, 52, was hurriedly pushed into a police van and driven away.

Sharma said Sobhraj's legal team planned to move a case of contempt of court against Delhi police. "This order cannot be just made a mockery," Judge Kumar said after learning that Sobhraj had been detained following his order.
Deputy police commissioner Pradeep Srivastava told Reuters that the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO), which issues papers to foreigners, had ordered Sobhraj detained.
"He claims he is a French citizen but he does not have valid documents," said a police official who asked not to be named.
Srivastava said the FRRO had ordered Sobhraj detained in the local Lodhi colony police station until March 2.

A French citizen born to an Indian father and a Vietnamese mother, Sobhraj told reporters last week that he feared re-arrest as he did not have valid papers authorising him to remain in India as a foreigner.
He had said he planned to go directly from the court to the French embassy to obtain papers after being released on bail.

Earlier Kumar, issuing the order to release Sobhraj, said there was no reason to keep him in jail as he had provided bail in the two outstanding cases against him. "There is no reason for him to be in jail," Kumar said.
One case concerned a lapsed Thai extradition request, while the other stemmed from a 1986 jailbreak which earned Sobhraj fame. India courts are expected to take up both cases soon.
"I feel great, like I'm born again," Sobhraj told reporters minutes before he was detained.

Sobhraj was first arrested in India for holding up a hotel jewellery shop in 1971. He has since been charged with a long string of crimes including murder, serving time for some and winning acquittal in others.

Before being detained, Sobhraj told reporters he wanted to say a prayer while heading to the French embassy to obtain identity papers. Asked if he would revert to crime, Sobhraj said: "Never. Never ever."
But as he emerged from court, Sobhraj was engulfed by police and whisked away.
Last week Sobhraj, who says he has converted to Buddhism, said he wanted to turn to social work after leaving prison and could work on a $15-million movie based on his life.
He said he planned to stay in India for a few months before going to France. "I have to watch my step carefully," he said.
